title: Retained EU law becomes assimilated law
subtitle: The EUWA 2018 snapshot, the REUL Act 2023 rewrite, and what actually changed on 1 January 2024
objectives: Explain what the European Union (Withdrawal) Act 2018 actually did — freezing a snapshot of EU law into domestic law, not simply 'keeping EU law'

Distinguish the REUL Act 2023's scheduled revocation approach from the blanket 'sunset' it replaced, and state what changed for supremacy, general principles and Francovich damages from 1 January 2024
Apply the correct label and legal status ('assimilated law') to a piece of formerly-retained EU law on a post-2024 fact pattern, without conflating the 2018 snapshot with the 2023 changes

leadingAuthorities.role: Creates the 2018 snapshot: converts direct EU law, preserves domestic implementing law, and (originally) retains supremacy and general principles

leadingAuthorities.citation: Retained EU Law (Revocation and Reform) Act 2023, ss 1–2
leadingAuthorities.role: Abandons the blanket sunset; replaces it with a scheduled revocation list (Schedule 1) and a rebrand to 'assimilated law'

leadingAuthorities.citation: Retained EU Law (Revocation and Reform) Act 2023, ss 4–6
leadingAuthorities.role: Ends supremacy over post-2024 domestic legislation and ends free-standing general principles and Francovich damages from 1 January 2024

whyThisMattersTemplate.default: This is one of only two lessons in this module testing genuinely current, still-changing UK statute law — and it's the one students most often get backwards, because the 2018 Act and the 2023 Act did almost opposite things to the same body of law. Where the profile shows knowledge ahead of application, this note appears: 'You can probably describe both Acts. The exam question is which one governs the fact pattern in front of you.'

profileHooks.weakApplication: You know the two Acts by name. The test pool here leans hard on application: expect a post-2024 fact pattern where you have to work out whether supremacy, a general principle, or a Francovich claim is even still available.
profileHooks.weakKnowledge: Slow down on Part 1 and Part 2 before anything else. If you can't yet say, without hesitating, which Act did the freezing and which Act did the thawing, the rest of this lesson will blur into one undifferentiated mass of 'Brexit law'.

overview.hook: On 31 December 2020, an enormous body of EU law was still, technically, part of English law. Three years later, most of it had a new name, a demoted legal status, and a chunk of it had simply vanished by operation of a schedule most practitioners had to look up. This lesson is about two Acts, three years apart, that did almost opposite things — and why conflating them is the single most common mistake examiners see on this topic.
overview.lawStatedNotice: Law stated as at 1 September 2026. This lesson covers genuinely live and recently-changed UK statute law, flagged with a caution symbol in the syllabus for that reason. The substance is settled: the REUL Act 2023 abandoned the original blanket 'sunset' (automatic revocation of all unlisted retained EU law at the end of 2023) in favour of a scheduled revocation list under Schedule 1; it ended the supremacy of retained EU law over post-2024 domestic legislation; and it ended free-standing general principles of EU law and Francovich damages for UK purposes from 1 January 2024, with retained EU law renamed 'assimilated law'. Commentary is consistent on all of that substance. It is markedly less consistent on the exact section-by-section mapping of these changes within the 2023 Act — this lesson's citations to specific sections should be treated as approximate and checked directly against legislation.gov.uk by a qualified lawyer before being relied on for precise drafting or advice, rather than taken as a verified pinpoint citation.

parts.heading: 2018: the snapshot, not the shutdown
parts.voice: mechanics-focused — walks through exactly what the Act did, step by step, before any evaluation
body: Start with a date and a mental image. At 11pm on 31 December 2020 — the end of the Brexit transition period — the European Union (Withdrawal) Act 2018 took a photograph of EU law as it stood at that instant, and converted what it saw into a new category of domestic law called 'retained EU law'.

It is worth being precise about what got photographed, because the Act does three different jobs in ss 2–4, not one. Section 2 preserves EU-derived domestic legislation — UK statutory instruments that had implemented directives, which would otherwise have fallen away for lack of a live EU law behind them. Section 3 converts 'direct EU legislation' — regulations, and directly effective decisions — straight into domestic law, since these had never needed a UK implementing instrument to begin with. Section 4 saves directly effective rights arising under the treaties and existing case law, catching anything the first two sections missed.

Section 5 and Schedule 1 then did something that, at the time, looked like the headline: they preserved the *supremacy* of this retained EU law over other domestic law made before exit day, and preserved free-standing general principles of EU law (such as proportionality and legal certainty) as an interpretive aid. Section 6 kept pre-exit CJEU case law binding as a matter of domestic precedent, while cutting UK courts off from making new references to Luxembourg.

Hold that picture for a moment: as of 2018, retained EU law was frozen in place, still supreme over older UK statutes, still coloured by general principles, still readable through pre-exit CJEU judgments. Nothing about the 2018 Act, on its own, reduced the status of this body of law. That reduction is a separate Act, three years later — and confusing the two is the trap this whole lesson exists to dismantle.

components.definition: The body of EU-derived law converted into domestic law by the European Union (Withdrawal) Act 2018 as at the end of the transition period (31 December 2020) — a snapshot, not an ongoing relationship with EU law-making.

interaction.prompt: The European Union (Withdrawal) Act 2018 converted EU law into UK law as it stood on which date?
options: 31 December 2020, the end of the transition period
23 June 2016, the date of the referendum
1 January 2024, when the REUL Act took effect
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Right — the 2018 Act's conversion happens at the end of the transition period, not at the referendum and not at any later reform date.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: The 2018 Act's conversion point is the end of the transition period, 31 December 2020 — the referendum date and the 2024 reform date both matter to this story, but not for this step.

parts.heading: 2023: the sunset that didn't happen — and the list that did
parts.voice: mechanics-focused — states the original plan clearly, then shows exactly how and why it was replaced
body: The Retained EU Law (Revocation and Reform) Act 2023 started life as a much blunter instrument than the one that reached the statute book. As introduced, the Bill proposed a blanket 'sunset clause': every piece of retained EU law not expressly preserved would automatically fall away at the end of 2023, full stop, regardless of whether anyone had checked what would be lost.

That approach drew sustained criticism — from practitioners, regulators and government departments themselves — on the basis that nobody had a complete, reliable inventory of everything the sunset would catch, and that automatic deletion of law nobody had reviewed was a serious rule-of-law risk. The government changed course during the Bill's passage.

What was enacted instead, in s 1 of the 2023 Act, reverses the default: rather than everything being revoked unless saved, only the instruments specifically listed in Schedule 1 are revoked at the end of 2023, and everything else survives by default, subject to ongoing departmental review and reform powers under later sections of the Act. This is the single most important structural fact in this lesson: **the sunset was abandoned in favour of a scheduled revocation list.**

Get this backwards — assuming a 2023-era blanket wipe actually happened — and every downstream answer about what survives, what changed status, and what simply vanished will be wrong. The list approach means the safe default assumption for an exam fact pattern is that a given piece of retained EU law is *still there*, just under a new label and a lower legal status, unless the facts tell you it was on the Schedule 1 list.

components.label: Two mechanisms, not one — do not merge them
points: The Bill as introduced: automatic sunset — everything not saved is revoked at end of 2023, by default
The Act as passed (s 1): scheduled revocation — only instruments named in Schedule 1 are revoked; everything else survives by default
Why the change: no reliable, complete inventory existed of everything the blanket sunset would have caught
Practical consequence: the presumption for an exam fact pattern is survival with a changed status, not automatic disappearance

interaction.prompt: Which statement correctly describes what the REUL Act 2023, as enacted, does to unlisted retained EU law?
options: It automatically revokes it at the end of 2023 unless expressly saved
It survives by default; only instruments specifically listed in Schedule 1 are revoked
It transfers it wholesale into a new EU-UK treaty framework
interaction.trapExplanation: Option 1 describes the original Bill's blanket sunset clause — the very mechanism Parliament rejected during the Bill's passage. The Act that was actually enacted flips the default: survival unless scheduled, not revocation unless saved. This is the most commonly confused point in the whole topic.

parts.heading: What 1 January 2024 actually switched off
parts.voice: mechanics-focused — itemises each specific legal effect that ended, resisting vague generalisation
body: Revocation by list is only half of the REUL Act 2023's work. The other half — and the part most often tested — is what it did to the *legal character* of the retained EU law that survived. Three distinct things ended on 1 January 2024, and they are worth holding apart precisely because students tend to mash them into one undifferentiated 'EU law lost its power' idea.

First: supremacy. Retained EU law had, since 2018, taken priority over inconsistent UK legislation passed *before* exit day. From 2024, that priority ends for legislation passed after the end of 2023 — assimilated law no longer trumps newer domestic statutes the way it once trumped older ones, and courts read assimilated law and later domestic legislation using ordinary rules of interpretation rather than an automatic EU-law override.

Second: general principles. The free-standing general principles of EU law — proportionality, legal certainty, fundamental rights as EU-law concepts — stop being available as an independent basis for disapplying legislation or grounding a claim in UK law from 1 January 2024. They can still inform how a surviving provision is interpreted where they were always baked into that provision's own text or purpose, but they no longer float free as an independent legal tool.

Third: Francovich damages. The route to suing the state for loss caused by a failure to properly implement EU law — the Francovich cause of action — ends for UK purposes from the same date. A claimant can no longer bring a fresh Francovich-style claim grounded in a post-2023 assessment of a historic implementation failure.

Finally, the rebrand: from this point, the body of surviving law is officially renamed 'assimilated law' rather than 'retained EU law' — a labelling change that signals the shift from 'EU law temporarily domesticated' to 'ordinary domestic law with an EU-derived history'.

components.citation: Retained EU Law (Revocation and Reform) Act 2023, ss 4–6 (section numbering approximate — see this lesson's currency notice)
components.text: Provisions ending the principle of supremacy for retained EU law over domestic legislation enacted after 2023, ending the status of retained general principles of EU law as a free-standing source of UK law, and ending the domestic Francovich damages cause of action, each with effect from 1 January 2024; and renaming retained EU law as assimilated law.
elements: Supremacy over post-2024 domestic legislation ends
Free-standing general principles cease to have independent effect from 1 Jan 2024
Francovich damages cease to be available for UK purposes from 1 Jan 2024
Retained EU law is renamed assimilated law

interaction.prompt: A claimant wants to argue, in litigation begun in 2026, that the UK failed to properly implement a pre-2021 directive and that this caused them loss. Tap the fact that determines whether a Francovich-style claim is available.
interaction.scenarioText: The alleged implementation failure occurred in 2019, while the directive was still in force. The claimant only discovered their loss in 2025 and issues a claim in 2026, relying on the Francovich principle as it applied under the 2018 Act's preserved general principles.
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Right. The date of the underlying failure isn't what matters here — the Francovich route was ended for UK purposes from 1 January 2024. A claim issued in 2026 cannot rely on it, whatever the vintage of the alleged breach.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Look at when the claim is actually brought, not when the underlying failure happened. Francovich damages stopped being available for UK purposes from 1 January 2024 — a 2026 claim falls after that cut-off regardless of how old the breach is.

parts.heading: Snapshot vs rewrite: telling the two Acts apart under pressure
parts.voice: Socratic — poses the classic confusion directly and works through it
body: Here is the question that catches almost everyone at least once: 'the 2018 Act gave EU law supremacy — so doesn't that mean the 2018 Act is still what makes retained EU law special today?' The honest answer is: it depends entirely on what year you're asking about, and that's exactly the kind of question this lesson trains you to answer precisely rather than vaguely.

For anything happening *before* 1 January 2024, the 2018 Act's settlement is still the right frame: supremacy over pre-exit legislation, general principles as an interpretive tool, pre-exit CJEU case law binding as precedent. For anything happening *on or after* 1 January 2024, the 2023 Act has overwritten the supremacy and general-principles parts of that settlement — though it has not touched s 6 of the 2018 Act's rule that pre-exit CJEU judgments remain binding domestic precedent, which is a separate strand the 2023 Act leaves largely alone.

The safest way to hold this in your head for an exam: the 2018 Act answers 'what law survived exit, and in what form?' The 2023 Act answers 'what happened to that surviving law's *status*, two questions later — did it get deleted, and did it lose its special powers?' Two different Acts, two different questions, applying to two different time periods either side of 1 January 2024.

components.title: Which Act governs — a decision path
components.description: A flowchart for classifying a fact pattern about retained/assimilated EU law by date and by question type.

nodes.label: Is the question about whether a specific instrument survived at all?
Check REUL Act 2023 Sch 1 — was it specifically listed for revocation at end of 2023?
Not listed → it survives by default, now called assimilated law
Listed → it was revoked at end of 2023
Is the question about supremacy, general principles or Francovich damages?
Event/claim before 1 Jan 2024 → 2018 Act settlement applies (supremacy over pre-exit law, general principles as interpretive tool)
Event/claim from 1 Jan 2024 → 2023 Act applies: no supremacy over newer legislation, no free-standing general principles, no Francovich

components.textAlternative: First decide whether the question is about survival (did an instrument get deleted?) or status (does it still carry supremacy, general principles, or Francovich?). For survival, check Schedule 1 of the REUL Act 2023: if the instrument is listed, it was revoked at the end of 2023; if not, it survives by default as assimilated law. For status questions, check the date: before 1 January 2024, the 2018 Act's settlement applies (supremacy over pre-exit legislation, general principles as an interpretive tool); from 1 January 2024 onwards, the 2023 Act applies and none of supremacy, free-standing general principles, or Francovich damages remain available.

interaction.prompt: How confident are you that the 2018 Act's rule keeping pre-exit CJEU case law binding as domestic precedent was itself removed by the 2023 Act?
interaction.explanation: The 2023 Act targets supremacy, free-standing general principles and Francovich damages. It does not repeal the separate rule in the 2018 Act that pre-exit CJEU judgments remain binding as a matter of domestic precedent — that strand is a distinct part of the 2018 settlement and survives the 2023 reforms largely intact.

parts.heading: Putting it on the exam page: naming, dating, and not overclaiming
parts.voice: direct — sets up the trap the tests will probe, and models careful exam phrasing
body: Two habits separate a strong answer on this topic from a weak one. The first is naming discipline: call the pre-2024 body of law 'retained EU law' when describing the 2018 position, and 'assimilated law' when describing anything from 1 January 2024 onwards. Using the terms interchangeably across a time boundary reads, to an examiner, exactly like the confusion this lesson is designed to prevent.

The second is resisting the urge to overclaim precision you don't have. This is genuinely live, recently-amended statute law, and even experienced commentators disagree on some of the fine section-by-section detail of the 2023 Act — a careful answer states the substance confidently (sunset abandoned for a scheduled list; supremacy, general principles and Francovich ended from 1 January 2024; the rebrand to assimilated law) without pretending to a false certainty about the exact clause number behind each change.
Put together, the two habits produce the kind of answer examiners reward: dated, correctly labelled, and honest about where the settled substance ends and the fine print begins.

components.commonWrongAnswer: Students often write that 'the 2023 Act sunset all retained EU law at the end of 2023', treating the abandoned Bill proposal as if it were the enacted law.
components.whyItsWrong: The blanket sunset was the proposal in the Bill as introduced, not the mechanism Parliament actually passed. The REUL Act 2023 as enacted reverses that default: only instruments specifically listed in Schedule 1 were revoked, and everything else survived — just under a new name and with reduced legal status. Writing that 'everything was sunset' will mislabel the single largest structural fact in this topic.

interaction.prompt: A UK statutory instrument implementing a pre-exit EU directive was never listed in Schedule 1 of the REUL Act 2023. A dispute arises in 2026 about whether it still overrides a UK statute passed in 2025. What is the correct analysis?
options: The instrument was automatically revoked at the end of 2023 because it wasn't expressly saved, so there is nothing left to apply
The instrument survives as assimilated law, but from 1 January 2024 it no longer takes priority over the 2025 statute purely by virtue of its EU-derived origin
The instrument still takes automatic priority over the 2025 statute because retained EU law is always supreme
interaction.explanation: Not being on Schedule 1 means the instrument survived — the sunset-everything-unless-saved approach was abandoned. But surviving is not the same as keeping its old powers: from 1 January 2024 it no longer has automatic supremacy over later domestic legislation, so the 2025 statute is not simply overridden by virtue of the instrument's EU-derived origin.

testPool.prompt: Name the Act that converted EU law into UK domestic law at the end of the Brexit transition period, and the Act that later changed that law's status from 1 January 2024.
acceptableAnswers: European Union (Withdrawal) Act 2018 and Retained EU Law (Revocation and Reform) Act 2023
testPool.modelAnswer: The European Union (Withdrawal) Act 2018 converted EU law into retained EU law at the end of the transition period; the Retained EU Law (Revocation and Reform) Act 2023 later revised its status from 1 January 2024.

testPool.prompt: What is the new official name for surviving retained EU law from 1 January 2024?
options: Assimilated law
Transitional law

testPool.prompt: Which of the following was NOT ended by the REUL Act 2023 from 1 January 2024?
options: Supremacy of retained EU law over post-2024 domestic legislation
Free-standing general principles of EU law
The binding status of pre-exit CJEU case law as domestic precedent
Francovich damages for UK purposes
testPool.trapExplanation: It is tempting to assume the 2023 Act swept away everything EU-related, but the 2018 Act's separate rule keeping pre-exit CJEU judgments binding as domestic precedent was not repealed by the 2023 reforms.

testPool.prompt: Put these events in chronological order.
items: Transition period ends; retained EU law is created
REUL Act 2023 as introduced proposes a blanket sunset
Supremacy, general principles and Francovich damages end; rebrand to assimilated law takes effect

testPool.prompt: How does the REUL Act 2023 as enacted differ from the blanket sunset clause originally proposed in the Bill?
options: The enacted version revokes only instruments listed in Schedule 1, reversing the default from revocation-unless-saved to survival-unless-listed
The enacted version is identical to the original proposal, just delayed by a year
The enacted version applies only to case law, not legislation

testPool.prompt: In the passage below, highlight the sentence that states what changed about supremacy.
testPool.passage: Retained EU law had, since 2018, taken priority over inconsistent UK legislation passed before exit day. From 2024, that priority ends for legislation passed after the end of 2023. Courts now read assimilated law and later domestic legislation using ordinary rules of interpretation rather than an automatic EU-law override.
testPool.ratioSentence: From 2024, that priority ends for legislation passed after the end of 2023.

testPool.prompt: A litigant in 2026 wants to invoke a free-standing EU general principle of proportionality, independent of any surviving statutory text, to challenge a piece of assimilated law. Can they do this?
options: No — free-standing general principles ceased to have independent effect for UK purposes from 1 January 2024
Yes — general principles were preserved permanently by the 2018 Act
Yes, but only in relation to competition law
testPool.explanation: Free-standing general principles stopped being an independent source of UK law from 1 January 2024. Proportionality may still matter where it is built into the wording or purpose of a surviving provision, but it cannot be invoked as a free-standing ground on its own from that date.

testPool.prompt: A regulator relies on a piece of retained EU law dating from 2019 in a 2026 enforcement decision. The instrument was never listed on Schedule 1 of the REUL Act 2023. What is its status?
options: It no longer exists, having been swept away by the sunset clause
It survives as assimilated law, though it no longer carries automatic supremacy over later domestic statutes
It still functions exactly as it did in 2019, unaffected by either Act
testPool.explanation: Not being listed means it survived the scheduled revocation. But surviving does not mean unchanged status — from 1 January 2024 it lost automatic supremacy over later domestic legislation, among other changes.

testPool.prompt: Tap the fact that tells you the 2018 supremacy settlement, not the 2023 reforms, governs this dispute.
testPool.scenarioText: A company argues in 2026 that a piece of retained EU law should have overridden an inconsistent UK statute passed in 2019, based on the legal position as it stood in 2022 when the alleged conflict first arose and was litigated to a final judgment before 2024.
tappableSpans: legal position as it stood in 2022
litigated to a final judgment before 2024
testPool.correctSpan: litigated to a final judgment before 2024
testPool.explanation: What matters for which regime applies is the date of the relevant legal event, not the date the argument is later made. A dispute resolved to final judgment before 1 January 2024 falls under the 2018 Act's supremacy settlement, even if it is discussed again in 2026.

testPool.prompt: Which scenario correctly applies the post-2024 position on Francovich-style claims?
testPool.scenarioA: A claimant issues a claim in 2026 seeking damages from the UK government for an EU-law implementation failure, relying on the Francovich principle as previously available under the 2018 Act's preserved general principles.
testPool.scenarioB: A claimant issued a claim in 2023, before the REUL Act 2023's changes took effect, relying on Francovich damages for a pre-exit implementation failure.
testPool.explanation: Francovich damages were ended for UK purposes from 1 January 2024. A claim issued in 2023, before that cut-off, could still rely on the principle; a fresh claim issued in 2026 cannot.

testPool.prompt: A student writes: 'The REUL Act 2023 sunset all retained EU law at the end of 2023, and only a short saved list survived.' Is this an accurate description of the Act as enacted?
options: No — it reverses the mechanism: only a scheduled list was revoked, and everything else survived by default
Yes — this is exactly what the enacted Act does

testPool.prompt: A UK regulator applies a piece of assimilated law (originally an EU regulation, never listed on REUL Act 2023 Schedule 1) to disapply a UK statute passed in 2025, on the basis that the assimilated law is 'EU law and therefore supreme'. Analyse whether this reasoning is correct.
factsToOrder: The instrument originates as an EU regulation converted by the 2018 Act
It was never listed on Schedule 1 of the REUL Act 2023
The regulator seeks to disapply a UK statute passed in 2025
The regulator's stated reason is that EU-derived law is automatically supreme

scaffolds.support: Full model IRAC answer shown, with each fact mapped to Issue / Rule / Application / Conclusion
Rule and Issue given; student drags facts into Application and writes Conclusion
Issue given only; student selects the Rule, drags facts into Application, writes Conclusion
No scaffold; student writes full IRAC unaided

modelAnswer.issue: Whether a surviving piece of assimilated law can be used to disapply a UK statute passed in 2025 on the ground of automatic supremacy.
modelAnswer.rule: Surviving retained EU law (now assimilated law) that is not listed on Schedule 1 of the REUL Act 2023 continues to exist, but from 1 January 2024 it no longer has automatic supremacy over UK legislation enacted after 2023 (REUL Act 2023).
modelAnswer.application: The instrument survives because it was never scheduled for revocation. But the regulator's reasoning conflates survival with retained supremacy — those are two separate questions. Because the 2025 statute post-dates the end of the supremacy rule, the assimilated law cannot automatically override it purely by virtue of its EU-derived origin.
modelAnswer.conclusion: The regulator's reasoning is incorrect. The instrument survives as assimilated law but cannot be used to automatically disapply the 2025 statute; supremacy over post-2024 legislation ended on 1 January 2024.

testPool.prompt: Why did Parliament move away from the blanket sunset clause originally proposed for the REUL Act 2023?
options: Because the CJEU ruled the sunset clause unlawful
Because there was no complete, reliable inventory of everything the automatic sunset would catch, creating a rule-of-law risk
Because the sunset clause was found to be incompatible with the Withdrawal Agreement
testPool.trapExplanation: Neither the CJEU nor the Withdrawal Agreement drove this change — the UK is not bound by CJEU rulings post-exit for this purpose. The real reason was domestic: the absence of a reliable inventory of everything an automatic sunset would delete.

testPool.prompt: In the passage below, highlight the sentence identifying the rebrand introduced by the REUL Act 2023.
testPool.passage: The REUL Act 2023 changed both the survival mechanism and the legal status of this body of law. Supremacy over post-2024 legislation ended, as did free-standing general principles and Francovich damages, all from 1 January 2024. From this point, the surviving body of law is officially renamed 'assimilated law' rather than 'retained EU law'.
testPool.ratioSentence: From this point, the surviving body of law is officially renamed 'assimilated law' rather than 'retained EU law'.

debriefConfig.trapSummary: The single most common mistake in this lesson's test items is treating the REUL Act 2023 as if it enacted the blanket sunset clause it was introduced with. It didn't — Parliament replaced the sunset with a scheduled revocation list, so the safe default for a fact pattern is survival with reduced status, not automatic deletion.
